# Assessment source restrictions — Debate 279

The controller read all 3,000 canonical events. Assess the available substantive recording from 55,760 to 6,240,960 ms, excluding 2,467,520–2,500,640 ms (41:07.52–41:40.64). The user expressly approved this 33.12-second exclusion after public captions and two paid transcription attempts failed to recover a reliable passage. Do not use either attempted reconstruction; they are not evidence. Neither speaker receives credit or a penalty for excluded words. Do not infer concession, evasion, absence of an argument or failure to answer from this interval. Both closing statements are present. Do not inherit another debate’s scope exception.

## Motion and burdens

The neutral motion is exactly “Does God exist?”. Matt Slick affirms it and explicitly elects to defend the Biblical Trinitarian God. Dan Barker defends atheistic nonbelief, stresses that withholding belief does not require proving universal nonexistence, and also advances particular incompatibility and evidential objections. Assess affirmative claims each actually adopts; do not force a universal disproof burden on every critical reply. Biblical claims are relevant to Slick’s chosen version of the affirmative case. A flaw in that version does not automatically disprove every possible god.

## Speaker ownership and phase boundaries

Named moderator handoffs and uninterrupted speeches establish Slick’s opening from approximately 00:55–20:13 and Barker’s from 20:33–40:53. Slick’s rebuttal resumes after the excluded interval and ends about 51:04; Barker’s runs about 51:20–61:54. Audience questions begin after the announced break about 62:33, normally with a two-minute answer and one-minute counter-response. They conclude about 94:07. Slick closes around 94:24–99:39 and Barker around 99:53–103:59. Verify exact event boundaries independently. Moderator and questioner premises are context, not claims automatically adopted by an advocate. Ideological fit alone is not attribution evidence. Mark unresolved ownership or load-bearing transcription uncertainty below high; do not force high confidence to avoid verification.

## Distinctions to preserve

Barker’s foreknowledge argument concerns God’s knowledge of God’s own future actions, and he repeatedly distinguishes that from human free will. An audience card later explicitly asks about human free will; preserve the actual question Slick answers rather than automatically treating his daughter analogy as an answer to a different question. Barker identifies himself as a compatibilist on human freedom. Slick distinguishes logic as reasoning from laws of logic as universal propositions, and moral grounding from the ability to behave well. Judge the forms they actually state.

Barker’s harm principle is a practical, species-relative guide, expressly not a universal law or a creed shared by every atheist. His argument from suffering and prayer is qualified: failed prayer does not alone disprove any conceivable God, and minimum harm avoidance allows positive compassion. His evolutionary altruism answer distinguishes an individual’s offspring from related genes and revises his wording about species; do not omit that qualification. Slick says his personal religious experience explains his commitment but explicitly denies offering that experience as proof. Both distinguish private motivation from public argument in relevant places; do not collapse them.

Slick’s first-cause argument contrasts a sufficient impersonal cause with personal choice; assess that actual bridge. Barker offers alternative cosmological possibilities and sometimes speaks more confidently of a multiverse while acknowledging missing observation; preserve both the claim and qualification. Do not import outside counterarguments or biographies. These source-fidelity notes do not prescribe ratings, move counts, success, failure, or tags. Read the whole source independently.

## Caption and selection cautions

Automatic captions contain errors in proper names, technical terms, citations and occasional phrasing. Do not silently correct an exact quote, or treat a caption error as a speaker’s mistake. Choose clear representative quotations and minimal complete supporting spans. Repetition, applause, jokes, illness, coughing, personal appearance, logistical exchanges and speaking fluency are not scored arguments. Both sides’ closing developments and substantive audience answers must receive full coverage consideration. Any newly discovered material source issue must be reported rather than concealed.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Now, tonight's topic, does God exist? All right. Well, I believe he does. Since I believe this, and I take the affirmative position in our debate, then the burden is upon me to at least try and demonstrate that God exists. I won't produce a microscope, get an X-ray machine in order to try and detect God's existence through some experimentation, some procedures. sourceSpan.excerpt: Well, I agree that logic is a function of the brain, but not just the brain. We both know that people can reason correctly. But how would you recognize correct reasoning if not by appealing to something outside the brain, such as the laws of logic, which guide proper reasoning? But these laws cannot be the product of the human brain. Otherwise, there is no way to determine if a person's reasoning is right or wrong. When the brain functions logically, it must be in harmony with the laws of logic. When the brain functions illogically, then it is not in harmony with those laws. But those laws are external to and independent of the brain since they govern it in regard to proper reasoning. Furthermore, the laws of logic are special kinds of propositions they since they are about truth. And that's one reason we know they require a mind because no material thing can be about another thing. Truth statements require minds.

moves.description: Slick argues that logical laws involve truth-bearing propositions yet remain valid independently of individual brains, so their stable authority is better grounded in a transcendent mind.

Principal limitation: The move slides from logical norms being independent of particular thinkers to their being thoughts in a transcendent thinker, without showing that abstract validity requires any mind or that divine cognition explains necessity. Live burden: He must defend the proposition ontology, explain how universal logical relations depend upon God without becoming contingent on divine psychology, and demonstrate why nondivine realist or naturalist accounts are inferior.

sourceSpan.excerpt: How does the atheistic perspective account for these laws? If the laws of logic are just functions of the human brain, as Mr. Barker stated, then that explanation cannot work because brains are different, and people contradict each other. Furthermore, if someone's physical brain causes him to deny the law of non-contradiction, that law is not invalidated. It's still true. Therefore, this proves that the logical thinking occurs in the brain, and the laws of logic do not depend upon human brains for their validity. If these logical laws are agreed-upon principles that people recognize as true, then they are recognizing principles that already exist. But how is it possible to have preexistent logical propositions in an atheistic worldview? And if it is people who declare these axioms to be true, then do the logical propositions become untrue when people decide they don't serve their subjective wants anymore? If these laws of logic are descriptions of natural phenomena, then how do you, for example, observe the law of proper inference in nature, which says if A equals B and B equals C, then A equals C without first presupposing the validity of the laws of logic which you used to deduce its truth. To do so is to beg the question. If these laws of logic are said to be properties of the universe, then they should be measurable since properties of the physical realm are quantifiable, whether they be things such as hardness, mass, polarity, or density. But you cannot apply this to the laws of logic. Furthermore, these laws of logic are characteristics that contain universality. They're true for everyone all the time. If you don't agree with the law of logic, the law of non-contradiction, it doesn't make it go away. We know that when people contradict themselves, we know they're just wrong. But these laws are there. They're not just a function of the brain. And they have a universality to them. They have a quality that applies to everyone all the time. They transcend it space and time. They have a transcendent characteristic. Now, which worldview best provides the rational justification for these transcendent universal truths? If the is Oh, man. Sorry. Is it the Christian worldview that proposes a transcendent mind that is the Christian God and who has revealed these universally true laws which are reflections of his perfect transcendent mind? Or are they the product of human brain action via evolution that assigned universal truth principles in the physical world and asserts them as a function of the physical brain? I assert that it's the former which makes sense and the atheistic perspective does not and cannot.

Live burden: He must establish that logical necessity cannot be primitive, structural, conceptual, or abstract, and then provide a discriminating bridge from whatever grounding mind follows to Trinitarian theism.
